explanation:
Braced initialization, which uses curly braces, is a C++11 feature designed to provide a more universal and consistent syntax for initializing objects. It aims to unify the different initialization forms that existed previously—parentheses and the equals sign—which had inconsistent rules and couldn't be used in all situations.

Scott Meyers makes a point to distinguish the conceptual goal, which he calls 'uniform initialization,' from the specific syntactic mechanism, which he calls 'braced initialization.' His key insight is that braces are the most versatile syntax available. They succeed in contexts where other forms fail, such as providing default values for non-static data members inside a class definition (where parentheses are illegal) or initializing uncopyable objects (where the equals-sign syntax is disallowed).

The mechanics of braced initialization allow it to be used for nearly every initialization scenario. It can be used for direct initialization, copy initialization, and aggregate initialization. This versatility means you can initialize an STL container with a list of elements, provide an in-class default member initializer, and construct uncopyable types like an atomic variable, all using the same clear, brace-based syntax. This consistency simplifies the language rules a programmer needs to remember.

In practical terms, this feature makes modern C++ code cleaner and more expressive. The ability to directly initialize containers with their contents is a major convenience that eliminates the need for repeated push_back calls. Standardizing on in-class member initializers improves encapsulation and ensures objects are always created in a valid state. By offering a single syntax that works for both copyable and moveable-only types, it simplifies writing generic code.

A common pitfall is assuming braced initialization is a perfect, drop-in replacement for all other initialization forms. As Meyers explores later, it has unique rules, particularly its strong preference for constructors taking an initializer list, which can lead to surprising behavior. Another mistake is being unaware of its advantages, causing developers to stick to older, more limited syntaxes out of habit.
practical_example: When defining a configuration class, you can use braced initialization to provide sensible default values for all member variables directly within the class definition, making the class easier to understand and ensuring instances are always properly initialized.
keywords: braced initialization, uniform initialization, C++ initializer list, curly brace initialization
